  <h1>How I Helped a Client Grow NRR from 101% to 105% in 6 Months</h1>
  <div class="post-meta">
    <span class="author">Will Sullivan</span>
    <span>April 17, 2026</span>
  </div>

<!-- ═══════════════════════════════════════ CONTENT ═══════════════════════════════════════ -->
<div class="post-content">
<p>A healthcare software company was preparing to go to market. Their NRR was 101% — technically above the 100% threshold, but not the kind of number that commands a premium multiple. Six months later, it was 105%. Here’s how we got there.</p>

<h2>What Did the Starting NRR Look Like?</h2>

<p>The company’s ARR Snowball told a clear story. Beginning NRR at 100%, with -4% churn, -3% product churn, -1% downsell, +3% upsell, and +6% cross-sell, ending at 101%.</p>

<p>The cross-sell number looked healthy at 6%, but it was masking a problem. The company had grown through a run of acquisitions, accumulating add-on products that customers didn’t want. That frustration was showing up as product churn — a leading indicator of full logo churn.</p>

<p>The <a href="/resources/board-quality-arr-snowballs/">ARR Snowball decomposition</a> revealed that the growth wasn’t durable. Cross-sell was high because the company kept pushing add-ons, but product churn and logo churn were eating the gains.</p>

<h2>2% Increase from Improving Upsell</h2>

<p>The first lever was pricing discipline — two straightforward operational changes:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>1% from annual CPI price increases on renewals.</strong> The company had never implemented automatic price escalation. We added a standard CPI increase to the renewal process. This is table stakes for net revenue retention, but many recurring-revenue companies skip it — especially those that grew through acquisition instead of organic GTM maturity.</li>
  <li><strong>1% from fixing revenue leakage.</strong> We found customers on outdated pricing — contracts that had auto-renewed for years without adjustment. Getting these customers onto current pricing recovered ARR that was already owed. consistently shows that pricing optimization is one of the fastest paths to NRR improvement.</li>
</ul>

<p>Neither of these required new products, new customers, or new GTM motions. Just operational rigor applied to existing customer relationships.</p>

<h2>Investigating Churn Drivers: The Product Churn Pattern</h2>

<p>The <a href="/resources/board-quality-arr-snowballs/">ARR Snowball analysis</a> uncovered a critical pattern: <strong>the majority of customers who churned had dropped a product (product churn) within twelve months before churning entirely.</strong></p>

<p>This wasn’t random. The acquired products were difficult to manage, and customers frustrated with them started looking at competitors’ offerings — and then switching.</p>

<p>The <a href="/resources/build-customer-data-cube-in-house-or-hire/">Customer Data Cube</a> made this pattern visible at the account-product level. Without account-product granularity, product churn and logo churn look like two separate problems. With it, the causal chain becomes clear: product frustration leads to product churn, which leads to logo churn.</p>

<h2>2% Increase from Addressing Product Churn</h2>

<p>The insight drove a counterintuitive recommendation: <strong>sunset products to grow NRR.</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li>We recommended sunsetting the weakest add-on products immediately, not at the end of the calendar year</li>
  <li>We initiated the sunsetting of the other 2 add-on products to be removed next quarter, before sell-side fireside chats started</li>
</ul>

<p>Less is more. By removing the products that were causing frustration, the company stopped the product churn → logo churn cascade. The short-term ARR hit from sunsetting was more than offset by the reduction in downstream churn.</p>

<p>We see this pattern repeatedly: rationalizing a product portfolio does more for retention than extending it.</p>

<h2>1% from Aligning the Data Story with the Growth Story</h2>

<p>The final lever was about how churn was presented, not how it was measured.</p>

<p>In the most recent acquisition, a cohort of customers had given notice that they would cancel because of the acquisition, but hadn’t formally churned yet. These were known future churners — M&A-related attrition, not organic business failure.</p>

<p>When building the sell-side data cube, we tagged and fenced off these customers to show their impact separately. This accomplished two things:</p>

<ol>
  <li>It removed ~1% of known M&A-related churn from the organic NRR number</li>
  <li>It highlighted the company’s sophistication in handling the complexities of acquiring and integrating bolt-on acquisitions</li>
</ol>

<p>The result: the organic growth story was cleaner and more defensible — exactly what a buy-side diligence team would want to see.</p>

<h2>The Impact: From 101% to 105%</h2>

<p>The ending NRR waterfall told a different story: -3% churn, -1% product churn, -1% downsell, +5% upsell, +5% cross-sell = <strong>105% ending NRR.</strong></p>
<p>Cross-sell came down a point, from +6% to +5%. That was the price of sunsetting two products, and we booked it deliberately: the cross-sell those products generated was the same revenue showing up two quarters later as product churn. Trading a point of cross-sell for two points of product churn is a good trade. A waterfall that hides the trade is not a waterfall a buyer will trust.</p>

<p>Three outcomes that mattered at exit:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Increased valuation multiple.</strong> Showing 5% organic growth put the company in a different category of comparable companies. NRR above 105% changes the conversation from “stable business” to “compounding business” — and the multiple reflects it.</li>
  <li><strong>Prepared for diligence.</strong> The CFO went into sell-side diligence with a clear, confident growth narrative instead of a defensive, explanation-laden position. Every number had a decomposition. Every movement had a driver.</li>
  <li><strong>Operational alignment.</strong> The data team learned to work with finance to drive strategic impact — a capability that transferred to the acquirer and added value beyond the transaction itself.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Why This Matters for Your Exit</h2>

<p>Every recurring-revenue company approaching exit faces the same question: can you prove that your growth is durable? An <a href="/resources/board-quality-arr-snowballs/">ARR Snowball</a> that decomposes NRR into its constituent movements — and connects those movements to operational decisions — is the difference between a story and a proof.</p>

<p>The moves that took this company from 101% to 105% weren’t complex. They were operational: price discipline, product rationalization, and data story alignment. But they required the right analytical foundation to identify, prioritize, and measure.</p>

<p>Every move here was done with the client’s team, not handed over as a report — which is why the capability transferred to the acquirer.</p>
</div>

  <h1>How I Helped a Client Grow NRR from 101% to 105% in 6 Months</h1>
  <div class="post-meta">
    <span class="author">Will Sullivan</span>
    <span>April 17, 2026</span>
  </div>
</div>

<!-- ═══════════════════════════════════════ CONTENT ═══════════════════════════════════════ -->
<div class="post-content">
<p>A healthcare software company was preparing to go to market. Their NRR was 101% — technically above the 100% threshold, but not the kind of number that commands a premium multiple. Six months later, it was 105%. Here’s how we got there.</p>

<h2>What Did the Starting NRR Look Like?</h2>

<p>The company’s ARR Snowball told a clear story. Beginning NRR at 100%, with -4% churn, -3% product churn, -1% downsell, +3% upsell, and +6% cross-sell, ending at 101%.</p>

<p>The cross-sell number looked healthy at 6%, but it was masking a problem. The company had grown through a run of acquisitions, accumulating add-on products that customers didn’t want. That frustration was showing up as product churn — a leading indicator of full logo churn.</p>

<p>The <a href="/resources/board-quality-arr-snowballs/">ARR Snowball decomposition</a> revealed that the growth wasn’t durable. Cross-sell was high because the company kept pushing add-ons, but product churn and logo churn were eating the gains.</p>

<h2>2% Increase from Improving Upsell</h2>

<p>The first lever was pricing discipline — two straightforward operational changes:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>1% from annual CPI price increases on renewals.</strong> The company had never implemented automatic price escalation. We added a standard CPI increase to the renewal process. This is table stakes for net revenue retention, but many recurring-revenue companies skip it — especially those that grew through acquisition instead of organic GTM maturity.</li>
  <li><strong>1% from fixing revenue leakage.</strong> We found customers on outdated pricing — contracts that had auto-renewed for years without adjustment. Getting these customers onto current pricing recovered ARR that was already owed. consistently shows that pricing optimization is one of the fastest paths to NRR improvement.</li>
</ul>

<p>Neither of these required new products, new customers, or new GTM motions. Just operational rigor applied to existing customer relationships.</p>

<h2>Investigating Churn Drivers: The Product Churn Pattern</h2>

<p>The <a href="/resources/board-quality-arr-snowballs/">ARR Snowball analysis</a> uncovered a critical pattern: <strong>the majority of customers who churned had dropped a product (product churn) within twelve months before churning entirely.</strong></p>

<p>This wasn’t random. The acquired products were difficult to manage, and customers frustrated with them started looking at competitors’ offerings — and then switching.</p>

<p>The <a href="/resources/build-customer-data-cube-in-house-or-hire/">Customer Data Cube</a> made this pattern visible at the account-product level. Without account-product granularity, product churn and logo churn look like two separate problems. With it, the causal chain becomes clear: product frustration leads to product churn, which leads to logo churn.</p>

<h2>2% Increase from Addressing Product Churn</h2>

<p>The insight drove a counterintuitive recommendation: <strong>sunset products to grow NRR.</strong></p>

<ul>
  <li>We recommended sunsetting the weakest add-on products immediately, not at the end of the calendar year</li>
  <li>We initiated the sunsetting of the other 2 add-on products to be removed next quarter, before sell-side fireside chats started</li>
</ul>

<p>Less is more. By removing the products that were causing frustration, the company stopped the product churn → logo churn cascade. The short-term ARR hit from sunsetting was more than offset by the reduction in downstream churn.</p>

<p>We see this pattern repeatedly: rationalizing a product portfolio does more for retention than extending it.</p>

<h2>1% from Aligning the Data Story with the Growth Story</h2>

<p>The final lever was about how churn was presented, not how it was measured.</p>

<p>In the most recent acquisition, a cohort of customers had given notice that they would cancel because of the acquisition, but hadn’t formally churned yet. These were known future churners — M&A-related attrition, not organic business failure.</p>

<p>When building the sell-side data cube, we tagged and fenced off these customers to show their impact separately. This accomplished two things:</p>

<ol>
  <li>It removed ~1% of known M&A-related churn from the organic NRR number</li>
  <li>It highlighted the company’s sophistication in handling the complexities of acquiring and integrating bolt-on acquisitions</li>
</ol>

<p>The result: the organic growth story was cleaner and more defensible — exactly what a buy-side diligence team would want to see.</p>

<h2>The Impact: From 101% to 105%</h2>

<p>The ending NRR waterfall told a different story: -3% churn, -1% product churn, -1% downsell, +5% upsell, +5% cross-sell = <strong>105% ending NRR.</strong></p>
<p>Cross-sell came down a point, from +6% to +5%. That was the price of sunsetting two products, and we booked it deliberately: the cross-sell those products generated was the same revenue showing up two quarters later as product churn. Trading a point of cross-sell for two points of product churn is a good trade. A waterfall that hides the trade is not a waterfall a buyer will trust.</p>

<p>Three outcomes that mattered at exit:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Increased valuation multiple.</strong> Showing 5% organic growth put the company in a different category of comparable companies. NRR above 105% changes the conversation from “stable business” to “compounding business” — and the multiple reflects it.</li>
  <li><strong>Prepared for diligence.</strong> The CFO went into sell-side diligence with a clear, confident growth narrative instead of a defensive, explanation-laden position. Every number had a decomposition. Every movement had a driver.</li>
  <li><strong>Operational alignment.</strong> The data team learned to work with finance to drive strategic impact — a capability that transferred to the acquirer and added value beyond the transaction itself.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Why This Matters for Your Exit</h2>

<p>Every recurring-revenue company approaching exit faces the same question: can you prove that your growth is durable? An <a href="/resources/board-quality-arr-snowballs/">ARR Snowball</a> that decomposes NRR into its constituent movements — and connects those movements to operational decisions — is the difference between a story and a proof.</p>

<p>The moves that took this company from 101% to 105% weren’t complex. They were operational: price discipline, product rationalization, and data story alignment. But they required the right analytical foundation to identify, prioritize, and measure.</p>

<p>Every move here was done with the client’s team, not handed over as a report — which is why the capability transferred to the acquirer.</p>
</div>
